title: In 2015, a prospector in Australia dug up a heavy reddish rock and hoped for gold inside. Three years later, a museum told him it was a 4.6-billion-year-old meteorite - Futura-Sciences

content:
The discovery dates back to May 2015. David Hole was prospecting with a metal detector in Maryborough Regional Park, approximately 1.2 miles south of the town, in the Australian state of Victoria. The region experienced a gold rush in the 19th century and remains popular with amateur gold prospectors.

He dug up an unusually heavy, reddish rock that he believed contained gold. However, the rock resisted every attempt to break it open, including a saw, an angle grinder, a drill, acid, and even blows from a sledgehammer.

A rock too heavy to be from Earth

Intrigued, he eventually took it to the Melbourne Museum in 2018. Two museum geologists, Dermot Henry and Bill Birch, almost immediately suspected it was a meteorite. Their attention was drawn to its density, which was considerably greater than that of a terrestrial rock of the same size, and its sculpted appearance, with small depressions covering its surface.

Such a quick identification was unusual. The museum regularly receives rocks that their owners believe to be meteorites. According to Dermot Henry, only two of all the specimens he had examined throughout his career had actually turned out to be meteorites.

The researchers used a diamond saw to remove a thin slice for analysis. Their findings were published in July 2019 in the Proceedings of the Royal Society of Victoria by Bill Birch, Dermot Henry, and geologist Andrew Tomkins.

An H5 ordinary chondrite

The meteorite measures approximately 15.4 inches long, 5.5 inches wide, and 5.5 inches thick. It belongs to the ordinary chondrite family, the most common type of meteorite, which generally originates in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter.

Chondrites take their name from chondrules, the small spherical silicate grains they contain. These grains, measuring up to one millimeter across in this specimen, formed when dust in the young solar system briefly melted during a sudden heating event before solidifying.

The letter H indicates a high iron content. The number 5 indicates that the rock underwent substantial heating within its parent asteroid: its matrix recrystallized, and the chondrules became less distinct. The main metallic minerals identified are iron-nickel alloys, including kamacite, taenite, and tetrataenite, often associated with an iron sulfide called troilite.

The analysis revealed no evidence of a violent shock experienced in space. Slight weathering appears in the form of thin layers of iron oxide surrounding the metallic grains, suggesting a relatively short period spent on Earth’s surface.

An unknown date of arrival

Carbon-14 dating indicates that the meteorite fell to Earth less than 1,000 years ago. No crater has been found. Local newspapers reported several meteor sightings in the region between 1889 and 1951, but none can be linked to the discovery site.

Its age of approximately 4.6 billion years corresponds to the formation of the solar system. Chondrites are among the oldest materials available for study and are slightly older than Earth itself.

Rarer than gold

The Maryborough meteorite is only the 17th meteorite recorded in the state of Victoria and the third H5 chondrite. It is also the second-largest single chondritic mass ever discovered in the state, after the Kulnine meteorite, which weighs approximately 121 pounds.

For the museum’s geologists, this rarity gives it a scientific value far greater than that of a gold nugget. Meteorites provide information about the age, formation, and chemical composition of the solar system. Some meteorites, belonging to different types than Maryborough, also contain organic molecules such as amino acids, or stardust grains older than the Sun.
